# Prescriptive lessons — howard-roberts × chord-melody

## close-voicing

Roberts treats close voicings as a deliberate textural minority — valuable precisely because they are uncommon. They earn their impact by punctuating an otherwise open-voiced texture, and serve equally as the raw material that octave displacement converts into open voicings. Within block chord writing, the choice between close and open density is left to the player's ear.

- [ch.3 p.12] Deploy close voicings sparingly — "very effective but not too often used" — as contrast against the open-voiced "big sound" that dominates chord melody texture.
- [ch.2 p.6] Convert any close voicing to an open voicing by moving one or more tones up or down an octave, "as far as your reach will permit" — the primary mechanism for expanding harmonic texture on guitar.
- [ch.2 p.8] In block chord style, both close and open voicings are permissible under each melody note; density choice belongs to the player's ear in context.

## open-voicing

Open voicings are the default sound of Roberts's chord melody language — the "big sound" against which everything else is measured. Two supporting doctrines keep them workable: harmonic memory permits chord tones to be dropped under sustain, and extensions may be freely added since they alter color without changing scale function.

- [ch.2 p.6 / ch.3 p.12] Open voicings, produced by octave-displacing one or more tones of a close position, constitute the dominant texture of solo guitar chord melody; close voicings exist as contrast against this baseline.
- [ch.2 p.9] When sustaining an open voicing through a long melody sequence, drop chord tones as fingering demands — sustain each tone "as long as physically possible before releasing" and rely on listener harmonic memory to complete what has been dropped.
- [ch.4 p.36] Add extensions (maj7, 6th, 9th) freely to any open voicing; they "only affect the color and texture of the chord" and do not alter its scale function or role in the progression.

## dom7b9

Roberts identifies the dominant 7b9 as a functional state that can be expressed through multiple surface spellings. Diminished chords whose tones overlap the dom7b9 spelling are valid chromatic substitutes; 6th chords can carry the same function when phrase context demands it.

- [ch.3 p.13] Substitute a diminished chord (e.g., E° or D♭°) for any dominant 7b9 (here, A7b9) to inject "chromatic relief from the monotony of diatonic lines" — valid wherever diminished tones overlap the dominant 7b9 spelling.
- [ch.3 p.12] A chord symbol does not determine function: "The G6 in bar 3 is functioning as a dominant chord (Eb+7b9)" — Roman numeral identity must be read from phrase context, not isolated spelling.

## dim7

Roberts uses diminished chords in two overlapping roles: as chromatic substitutes for dominant 7b9 sounds and as general chromatic passing connective tissue between diatonic points. Both applications are prescribed as ear-training material to be practiced in all keys.

- [ch.3 p.13] Use dim7 chords (E°, D♭°) as substitutes for dominant 7b9 sounds — specifically A7b9 in the cited example — to provide chromatic relief; practice in all keys with various diatonic melodies as active ear training.
- [ch.3 p.13] Beyond the dominant-substitute role, diminished shapes (alongside m7+5 forms) function as chromatic passing connective tissue between diatonic progression anchors; "It is good ear training to improvise this sort of thing in all keys, with various diatonic melodies."

## min7

Roberts's min7 usage spans three distinct contexts: upper-structure substitution for major-ninth chords, structural anchoring in diatonic passing-chord studies, and the universal sustain discipline that applies to all qualities. The sustain rule is not quality-specific but is explicitly illustrated in min7 contexts.

- [ch.2 p.8] In a block chord context, Gm7 substitutes for Eb maj9 — supplying its upper extensions (G=3, B♭=5, D=maj7, F=9) — making relative-minor upper-structure substitution a viable harmonization tool.
- [ch.3 p.11] Am7 and Bm7 anchor the diatonic skeleton of the passing-chord study (G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7), confirming min7 chords as stable harmonic targets against which altered passing shapes are measured.
- [ch.3 p.15] Apply the universal sustain rule to min7 voicings: keep root, minor third, fifth, and seventh ringing "until it's absolutely necessary to move them" — delay generates the continuity that defines chord melody style.

## maj7

Roberts names the major seventh as his first and clearest example of a color-only extension — one that can be reached for freely without disrupting harmonic grammar. Concurrently, Cmaj7 appears as a diatonic structural target (IV in G major) in the passing-chord study, confirming that maj7 voicings are fully stable harmonic destinations, not exotica.

- [ch.4 p.36] The major seventh is explicitly named as an extension that "only affect the color and texture of the chord" without changing scale function — reach for maj7 voicings freely wherever a major chord appears in the progression.
- [ch.3 p.11] Cmaj7 functions as the stable IV-position anchor in the diatonic passing-chord progression (G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7); it is a harmonic target, not a passing shape.

## 6

Roberts treats the 6th chord as a fully interchangeable color variant of its major triad or maj7 form for purposes of progression logic — yet simultaneously demonstrates that the same spelling can carry dominant 7b9 function in the right phrase context. Both lessons underscore his core claim that chord symbols are secondary to contextual analysis.

- [ch.4 p.36] The sixth is a color-only extension: "the addition of the extensions Maj. 7th, 6th, 9th, etc., only affect the color and texture of the chord" — the 6th chord is interchangeable with its triad or maj7 for harmonic grammar purposes.
- [ch.3 p.12] A G6 can carry dominant 7b9 function (functioning as Eb+7b9) when phrase context requires it — functional identity depends on full phrase analysis, never on isolated chord spelling.
- [ch.3 p.11] G6 anchors the tonic position (I in G major) in the diatonic passing-chord study, confirming the 6th voicing as a fully valid tonic chord quality in Roberts's harmonic vocabulary.

## add9

Roberts treats the ninth as a color-only addition requiring no special justification within chord melody arranging. A single authoritative statement covers it: extensions alter texture, not harmonic grammar.

- [ch.4 p.36] The ninth is explicitly named among extensions that "only affect the color and texture of the chord and do not change its scale function or its role in the progression" — add9 voicings may be inserted freely without altering the harmonic logic of the passage.

## min7b5

Roberts employs m7+5 shapes (the enharmonic neighbor of min7b5) as chromatic passing connective tissue between diatonic anchor chords — momentary dissonance is acceptable because the shapes serve a linking, not a landing, function.

- [ch.3 p.11] Altered passing shapes G#m7+5 and Am7+5 connect the primary diatonic chords (G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7) in the passing-chord study; these forms serve as chromatic connective tissue even when momentarily dissonant with the underlying harmony.

## aug

Augmented-fifth voicings appear in Roberts's method as passing shapes, not destinations. The m7+5 forms in the chapter 3 study and the broader principle in chapter 4 — that independent melodic and harmonic motion generates "interesting extensions" — together position the augmented quality as productive friction rather than a harmonic goal.

- [ch.3 p.11 / ch.4 p.40] M7+5 (minor seventh with augmented fifth) shapes function as chromatic linking texture between diatonic chords; the augmented quality is a passing state, and "interesting extensions" emerge when melody and harmony move with independent force.

## any

Several of Roberts's most important prescriptions are quality-neutral — they apply to every chord the player voices. These include the universal sustain rule, the chromatic melody harmonization policy, the physical register floor, and the block chord voicing discipline.

- [ch.3 p.15] Universal sustain rule: "Sustain each chordal tone for as long as possible… keep your fingers in place until it's absolutely necessary to move them" — this applies across all chord qualities and is the primary generator of chord melody continuity.
- [ch.4 p.38 / ch.4 p.40] Any chromatic melody note "can always be harmonized with a given chord form, although it may occasionally be dissonant" — when melody and harmony move independently, "interesting extensions" emerge from the friction.
- [ch.4 p.36] Hard register floor across all qualities: the melody may sit as low as the 4th string but no lower; when it falls below this floor, jump the melody up an octave rather than compromise the voicing.
- [ch.2 p.9] Block chord rule: change the voicing or inversion with each new melody note to "create the effect of all lines moving at once" — leaving the chord form static while the melody moves "tends to destroy the block chord effect."
- [ch.2 p.9] Proscriptive corollary: even when the melody "can be fingered easily without having to change the chord form," change it anyway — mechanical ease is not a valid reason to leave the voicing static.
- [ch.2 p.10] Short punctuations must be "played with authority and appropriately placed within the bar"; reinforce harmonic continuity further by choosing melodies that emphasize chord tones, letting the melodic line do harmonic work the sparse chord cannot do alone.
- [ch.4 p.42 / ch.4 p.52] Working method: arrange "as simply as possible," concentrate on voicings that "sound good to you and still permit the melody to be played," and repeat — simplicity is the starting constraint; repetition builds the instinct that eventually produces extemporaneous chord melody.
